query: AlCrFeNiSi belongs to a high-entropy-alloy family developed to combine properties that traditional single-principal-element alloys often cannot achieve simultaneously. Earlier research sought stable solid solutions and adjusted HEA compositions to target particular properties, but tradeoffs persisted: the CoCrFeMnNi system has limited wear and corrosion resistance, manganese can promote oxidation and oxide spallation, and cobalt-containing systems raise cost and processability concerns. Conventional bulk fabrication can cause compositional segregation during cooling, whereas mainstream metallic additive-manufacturing techniques can generate residual thermal stresses that impair mechanical performance and increase processing complexity. Given cobalt-free AlCrFeNiSi powder feedstock, what single intervention could improve mechanical integrity while limiting segregation, residual stress, and defect formation? State one hypothesis containing the intervention, its causal mechanism, a quantitative or directional outcome relative to conventionally fabricated AlCrFeNiSi, the processing and test boundaries of validity, the prior evidence supporting it, and a decisive experiment that could falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: In laser powder bed fusion (LPBF) processing of cobalt‐free AlCrFeNiSi, preheating the build substrate to an elevated temperature will reduce thermal gradients during solidification, thereby limiting compositional segregation, residual stresses, and defect formation, which in turn improves the mechanical integrity of the fabricated part.
generation.intervention: In‐situ substrate/build plate preheating during LPBF processing
generation.conditions: Fabrication using LPBF with controlled atmosphere; processing parameters (laser power, scan speed) held constant except for the incorporation of a defined preheat temperature
generation.structural_mediator: A more uniform cooling and solidification profile that minimizes steep thermal gradients
generation.mechanism: Preheating the build plate reduces the temperature differential between the melt pool and the surrounding material, which lowers the cooling rate. This in turn mitigates microsegregation during solidification, reduces residual thermal stress accumulation, and limits defect formation (such as cracking or porosity), all contributing to improved mechanical integrity.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared to conventionally processed (non-preheated) parts, preheated builds are expected to exhibit a more homogeneous microstructure, lower residual stresses, reduced segregation, and enhanced mechanical properties (e.g., higher yield strength and toughness). The improvement is directional; however, the exact magnitude remains uncertain and depends on the chosen preheat temperature and processing parameters.
generation.baseline: Conventionally fabricated AlCrFeNiSi parts produced by LPBF without substrate preheating
generation.boundary: This intervention is expected to be effective in LPBF processes under inert atmospheres with similar powder feedstock characteristics; its applicability to other additive manufacturing methods or significantly different processing regimes is unverified.
generation.uncertainty: While the reduction in thermal gradient and defect formation is anticipated, the optimal preheat temperature and the quantitative impact on mechanical properties are not precisely established and require further experimental calibration.

falsification_experiment.design: Process two sets of AlCrFeNiSi specimens via LPBF under identical laser parameters and inert atmosphere conditions: one set is manufactured with the build plate preheated to a target temperature (e.g., an optimized value based on preliminary trials) and the other set is produced without preheating. After fabrication, perform a systematic analysis including microstructural characterization (SEM with EDS for segregation assessment), residual stress measurement (using X-ray diffraction), and standardized mechanical tests (tensile, fatigue, and fracture toughness).
measurements: Microstructural homogeneity and grain size distribution via SEM/EDS
Mechanical properties such as yield strength, ultimate tensile strength, ductility, and toughness
Defect density (e.g., porosity, cracking) via radiographic methods or micro-CT
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the preheated samples do not show statistically significant improvements in residual stress reduction, reduced segregation and defect density, and enhanced mechanical properties relative to the non-preheated control group, then the hypothesis that in-situ build preheating improves mechanical integrity by mitigating segregation and residual stress in AlCrFeNiSi would be falsified.

cited_evidence.text:
Unlike other conventional alloys based on a “principal element,” high-entropy alloy (HEA) is a unique material that maintains a random solid solution structure without forming intermetallic compounds in operating temperatures due to its high configurational entropy [1] – [3] . It also has outstanding physical and chemical properties, which makes it a potential replacement for traditional metallic materials, and it has recently been referred to as a multi-principal element alloy (MPEA) or compositionally concentrated alloy (CCA) [4] – [9] .

As attention in HEAs increases, many studies have been conducted to explore its mechanical, physical and chemical properties [10] – [15] . In particular, equiatomic CoCrFeMnNi HEA, which was the first developed HEA, is the most studied because of its excellent combination of tensile strength and elongation along with excellent fracture toughness and corrosion resistance [6] , [16] – [21] . However, despite the advantages of equiatomic CoCrFeMnNi HEA, many issues arise owing to its low yield strength and costly and complex thermomechanical processing (i.e., multiple casting → hot rolling → homogenization → cold rolling → annealing → cutting, etc.

High-entropy alloys (HEAs) present a new approach of alloying concepts. Whereas conventional alloys usually comprise one major alloying element and minor additions of other alloying elements to improve properties, HEAs consist of at least five elements with close to equimolar composition. For several compositions, the desired formation of solely solid solutions with a face-centred cubic (fcc) or a body-centred cubic (bcc) structure could be achieved [ [1] , [2] , [3] ].

Several groups of HEAs have been intensively investigated. The term compositionally complex alloys (CCAs) was introduced for HEAs with a multiphase microstructure [ [4] ]. Several investigations prove the formation of primarily cubic phases in the alloy AlCoCrCuFeNi and its derivatives [ [5] , [6] , [7] ]. Aluminium strongly influences the microstructure, phase formation and resulting properties. Furthermore, aluminium acts as a stabiliser of bcc solid solutions and can suppress the formation of complex phases [ [8] , [9] , [10] ].
